title: Where Did Europe’s Countries—and the United Kingdom—Get Their Names?
description:
in History, Language |   	July 24th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

The typ­i­cal stu­dent trav­el­ing on a Eurail pass will stop in such lands as
body:
in History, Language |   	July 24th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

The typ­i­cal stu­dent trav­el­ing on a Eurail pass will stop in such lands as Öster­re­ich, Italia, Česko and Schweiz — also known as Suisse, Svizzera, and Svizra. If that stu­dent hap­pens to hail from the Eng­lish-speak­ing world, the names Aus­tria, Italy, the Czech Repub­lic (the recent move­ment for Czechia notwith­stand­ing), and Switzer­land will sound more famil­iar. But the ques­tion inevitably comes to mind while rid­ing between one his­tor­i­cal­ly and cul­tur­al­ly rich cap­i­tal to anoth­er: where did all these coun­tries get their names in Eng­lish? How on Earth, for exam­ple, did Deutsch­land, known in cer­tain oth­er Euro­pean lan­guages as Alle­magne, Ale­ma­nia, or Ale­man­ha, get to be called Ger­many?
Lan­guage YouTu­ber Rob­Words has an expla­na­tion. “To the Romans, it was the land of the Ger­mani, their name for the weird peo­ple speak­ing gib­ber­ish lan­guages to the east of the Riv­er Rhine,” he says in the video above, stand­ing in a for­est con­ve­nient­ly locat­ed in Ger­many itself.
They “also used the word ale­man­ni to describe a con­fed­er­a­tion of Ger­man­ic peo­ple, and that’s where a load of oth­er lan­guages get their word for Ger­many too.” And the mean­ing of Deutsch­land? “Land of the Dutch,” that last actu­al­ly being the descen­dant of an old Ger­man­ic word mean­ing ‘pop­u­lar’ or ‘peo­ple’ ” — which, before that time, referred not sim­ply to human beings, but the pop­u­la­tion who spoke the region’s wide­ly under­stood “pop­u­lar lan­guages.”


	

Behind most every Euro­pean coun­try’s Eng­lish name lies a sto­ry, if some­times an ambigu­ous, con­test­ed, and con­tro­ver­sial one. Most are also his­tor­i­cal­ly illu­mi­nat­ing: take Bel­gium, once con­sid­ered part of the Nether­lands (home of the peo­ple we now call Dutch), whose name derives from a tribe, or con­fed­er­a­tion of tribes, known in Latin as the Bel­gae: a word “adopt­ed by peo­ple liv­ing in the south­ern Low Coun­tries dur­ing the region’s strug­gle for inde­pen­dence from Spain in the six­teenth cen­tu­ry.” Rob­Words has more such sur­pris­ing facts to reveal in the video just above, in which he breaks down the names of all the coun­tries in the Unit­ed King­dom, cov­er­ing Ire­land, Scot­land, Wales, his native Eng­land, and also the word Britain itself, as well as the Great often attached to it. The lat­ter isn’t a boast, he stress­es, but rather a means of dis­tin­guish­ing the island from part of France. As for which part, you’ll have to watch to find out.

Based in Seoul, Col­in Marshall writes and broad­casts on cities, lan­guage, and cul­ture. He’s the author of the newslet­ter Books on Cities as well as the books 한국 요약 금지 (No Sum­ma­riz­ing Korea) and Kore­an Newtro. Fol­low him on the social net­work for­mer­ly known as Twit­ter at @colinmarshall.

title: 19th Century Japanese Woodblock Prints Creatively Illustrate the Inner Workings of the Human Body
description:
in Art |   	July 24th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			
Folks with a pass­ing knowl­edge of ukiyo‑e, the Japan­ese wood­block print art form pop­u­lar in
body:
in Art |   	July 24th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			
Folks with a pass­ing knowl­edge of ukiyo‑e, the Japan­ese wood­block print art form pop­u­lar in the 17th through 19th cen­turies, will be famil­iar with its land­scapes, as well as its por­traits of cour­te­sans and kabu­ki actors. But often these prints were edu­ca­tion­al, as demon­strat­ed by these very odd anatom­i­cal prints that pro­mote good health as it relates to our inter­nal work­ings.
Long before ani­mat­ed mon­sters warned us about our mucus-filled chests, Japan­ese artists like Uta­gawa Kunisa­da (1786–1865) filled the guts of these men and women with lit­tle work­ers, mak­ing sure the human body worked like a func­tion­ing vil­lage or town.
In the first print, Inshoku Yojo Kaga­mi (“Mir­ror of the Phys­i­ol­o­gy of Drink­ing and Eat­ing”), a man dines on fish and drinks sake. Inside, lit­tle men scur­ry about a pool wrapped in intestines, stoke a fire under the heart, all the while a schol­ar keeps ref­er­ence mate­ri­als near­by. Down below lone­ly fig­ures guard the “urine gate” and the “feces gate,” sure­ly one of the worst jobs in all the body econ­o­my.

One of Kunisada’s stu­dents cre­at­ed a print for the women, focus­ing on the repro­duc­tive organs, called Boji Yojo Kaga­mi (“Rules of Sex­u­al Life”). Keen-eyed view­ers will note that the minia­ture work­ers here are all women, so at least there’s some equal­i­ty at play.

The two prints were meant as instruc­tion­al, point­ing out best health prac­tices, and warn­ing against overindul­gence and excess.

Oth­er prints are just as inven­tive: a back and abdomen cov­ered in chil­dren play­ing famil­iar games; anoth­er fea­tur­ing pop­u­lar kabu­ki actors stand­ing in for var­i­ous organs. (Now, that is just cry­ing out for a mod­ern remake). The last print shows a preg­nant woman whose bel­ly con­tains Tainai jukkai no zu (Ten Realms with­in the body), a Bud­dhist idea that you can read more about here. As for their func­tion inside the womb, that is for oth­ers of a high­er con­scious­ness to dis­cern.

Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2019.
Relat­ed Con­tent:

title: Felicia Chiao's Domestic Scenes Reflect the Emotional Structures of Daily Life
description: “When I was really little, I wanted to be one of those stackable chairs you’d see in like a school auditorium,” Felicia Chiao says. “I thought the
body:
“When I was really little, I wanted to be one of those stackable chairs you’d see in like a school auditorium,” Felicia Chiao says. “I thought they looked cozy.” This childhood memory is the basis for a playful drawing in which Chiao’s signature characters mound atop one another. Layering reigns in this imagined world as calendars and clocks emerge from the wall in dense piles, while stacks of books and dishes rest on the floor. 
Chiao is known for her warm illustrations that capture emotion and the variances of mental health through surreal, flower-filled scenes. Working in pencil, ink, and watercolor, the artist renders compositions that feel both timeless and indicative of our current age, in which the anxieties and tribulations of life today emerge through curious characters.
“Stacks”
Alongside her largely domestic scenes, Chiao has also been adding to her growing collection of Lunar New Year drawings, which feature the animal of the year set against a gilded and crimson backdrop. 
Play and constraint also figure prominently into the artist’s approach. “I did a very cool collaboration with Heath Ceramics last year, and while it was a completely different medium than what I am used to, I think it has influenced my drawing process,” she says. “I’ve been experimenting with more mixed media (watercolor, color pencil, markers, sometimes a little gouache or gel pen).” The mats for frames are similar, as she enjoys the challenge of customizing the otherwise stark white material to complement her works.
This October, Chiao will open a solo show with Harman Projects and has several exhibitions slated for the coming years. She offers a variety of prints through her shop, and you can keep up with her latest works and collaborations on Instagram.

title: Damien Aubin Documents a Former Soviet Mining Settlement Suspended in Time
description: The small settlement of Pyramiden on the Norwegian archipelago of Svalbard is literally frozen in time. A former mining outpost for the Soviet Uni
body:
The small settlement of Pyramiden on the Norwegian archipelago of Svalbard is literally frozen in time. A former mining outpost for the Soviet Union, industrial operations ceased in 1998, and residents relocated. It wasn’t until 2007 that a handful of new inhabitants made the settlement home.
Because Pyramiden was abandoned in a cold climate, it remains impeccably preserved, with remnants of its once-thriving settlement still visible. French photographer Damien Aubin visited the Arctic region and documented the still, serene environment blanketed in snow. “The place has not been abandoned. It has been left in suspension,” he says. 
Classroom, Pyramiden
Pyramiden’s buildings and the objects inside are largely unchanged. Books sit open on school desks, and an unblemished statue of Lenin presides over a common area. Outside, a towering outdoor monument soars into the sky, the vibrant red and blue paint a stark contrast to the otherwise white landscape. 
“I photograph these environments at a distance, in a restrained, diffuse light. There is no event to describe, no narrative to unfold,” Aubin adds. “Across Pyramiden, Barentsburg and Longyearbyen, the same condition appears:spaces shaped by human intent, no longer aligned with it.”
Aubin has compiled the photos in a limited-edition book slated for release in September. You can purchase a copy on his website.

title: A New Colossal Shop Collection Highlights Local Artists and Chicago-Made Goods
description: Colossal has always called Chicago home. We love highlighting artists and designers in our own community, and the Colossal Shop’s newest collectio
body:
Colossal has always called Chicago home. We love highlighting artists and designers in our own community, and the Colossal Shop’s newest collection brings our creative neighbors to a wider global audience.
This selection features one-of-a-kind and handmade objects from Chicago-based artists we’re excited to share a city with. From unique ceramic forms to thoughtfully designed apparel, there’s something exciting for everyone.
Shop the collection now.

Periwinkle Ripple Mugs
With rhythmic, stacked silhouettes and looping handles, these one-of-a-kind mugs turn morning coffees into a sculptural experience. Created as a series of 8 exclusively for Colossal, each retro-futuristic mug is uniquely hand-thrown and assembled by Chicago ceramic artist Dara Schuman. Read more about her work here.




The Kami Bag
A chic reinterpretation of the quintessential brown paper grocery bag, the Kami Bag designed by Bukuro is handcrafted from richly textured leather and lined in a soft suede. Both a unique accessory and fascinating conversation piece, its familiar form is elevated through thoughtful construction and unexpected materials.




Miniature Ceramic Animals
Starting Projects creates the cutest, tiniest friends to keep you company. Adopt a creature to roam your desk, bookshelf, or trinket display. Or, surprise a loved one with a miniature version of their pet. We currently have eight breeds to choose from.




Seed Libraries and Agave Grow Kits
Immerse yourself in a new tale of growing your own herbs, vegetables, and desert plants inside your own abode. Founded by two regular thumb-colored people inside their Chicago home, Modern Sprout makes thoughtfully crafted products to simplify plants and indoor gardening.




Hats and Helping Hand Trays
What better way to express your enthusiasm for hats and dogs? Chicago-based artist Joe Kraft works with a variety of materials. While exploring ceramics, the artist creates design objects like the Helping Hand Tray—your daily dish for keys, rings, cash, and more. However, his love for drawing and printmaking drives his practice, which informs his line of apparel, including bright, fun dad caps.




Magic Wand Spoons and Swirl Star Incense Holders
Hand-built one at a time, these stoneware pieces are small but mighty. DAiLY SPECiAL—a small ceramics studio by multidisciplinary artist Lulu Luyao Chang—creates whimsical hand-built ceramics, jewelry, cups, and home goods that blend playful nostalgia with organic forms.




Emerging Artist Hats and Kiln Loader Totes
Artist and illustrator Molly Anne Bishop is inspired by nature, the mundane, and the boring, everyday things we all have to do. If you’ve ever loaded a kiln, you can probably relate to this awkward, quirky, puzzle-like process. And the Emerging Artist hat is a celebration of the potential inside of all of us and a tribute to our local cicada friends popping up to visit.



Silver Accessories
Why settle for plain hairstyles and ordinary lighters? Yard Sale Jewelry is the world of Ali Romero, a Chicago-based metals artist connected to organic forms and driven by a passion for transformation and natural elements.



Risograph Printed Matchboxes
Add some charm to your living room, kitchen, or bedside table. These small-batch risograph-printed matchboxes by Sunroom don playful illustrations of vibrant butterflies, cozy summer campfires, and striped edges, turning an everyday essential into a whimsical experience.
Find the full collection in the Colossal Shop.

title: A View From the Easel
description:
Community
                “Always in stock: coffee, beer, tequila, and that Swiss chocolate named Ragusa.”
body:
Community
                “Always in stock: coffee, beer, tequila, and that Swiss chocolate named Ragusa.”
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            Welcome to the 347th installment of A View From the Easel, a series in which artists reflect on their workspace. This week, Shahryar Nashat sculpts along to the sounds of Kelis's "Milkshake" and experiments with "a nautical glue the color of honey."Want to take part? Check out our submission guidelines and share a bit about your studio with us through this form! All mediums and workspaces are welcome, including your home studio.Shahryar Nashat, Asnières-sur-Seine, FranceHow long have you been working in this space?Three years this September. Although the space is similar to my former studio in Glendale, California, the journey couldn’t be different. Before, I drove by car through Laurel Canyon to the 101, then east on the 134 into Glendale. By the time you reached the studio, you’d already passed through a few different versions of Los Angeles. Here in Paris, it’s two wheels from the 11th, heading north through the 18th via République, watching the city thin out until you cross the Seine. Asnières-sur-Seine, just north of Paris, is also home to one of the first pet cemeteries in the world: le Cimetière des Chiens et Autres Animaux Domestiques.Describe an average day in your studio.Regular hours help structure the days and keep things moving when the direction of the work isn’t set yet. Always in stock: coffee, beer, tequila, and that Swiss chocolate named Ragusa (so close to a palindrome it hurts). Music is almost always on. Badalamenti’s Twin Peaks score only plays for difficult mold-making sessions. Lately it’s been ’90s: Erykah Badu, Lauryn Hill, Aaliyah, or Kelis. “I can teach you, but I have to charge.”How does the space affect your work?Making changes the work, but the inspiration never starts in the studio. The right tools, a good night’s sleep. That’s where it’s at. Light’s important too. This is what I miss from the West Coast days: the bright sunlight for forensic examinations and the roll-up gate. Scrolling it down was always a ritual, the sound of the day ending, whether it was a good one or if it all went to shite.How do you interact with the environment outside your studio?There are a handful of other artists in the building. All good people. My good friend Cooper Jacoby has a space here too. We have coffee and exchange notes on silicone cure times.What do you love about your studio?The proximity to Nouilles Fraîches Tibétaines on avenue Laurent Cély. The name speaks for itself. Fresh, homemade, and delicious. The same satisfaction as a burrito from El Sauz Tacos with Gabriel, at the corner of Chevy Chase and San Fernando Road.What do you wish were different?A little less warm in the summer, a little less cold in the winter.What is your favorite local museum?The Gustave Moreau Museum. Former studio, now museum, or mausoleum … all in one. This place is absurd. The main gallery is two stories tall with a massive skylight, and the walls are completely covered with paintings and drawings. It’s overwhelming in the best way. André Breton called it the most moving of all museums.What is your favorite art material to work with?Papier-mâché. A nautical glue the color of honey. More recently, Fabrican: a spray-on fabric that made its way down a bridal runway on Bella Hadid at Paris Haute Couture Fashion Week a couple years ago, and which I used to “dress” the Mothers sculptures currently on show at Gladstone on 64th Street in Manhattan. All are studio regulars. Oh, and anything acrylic by Golden.

title: Trump Installs Thomas Jefferson Statue in the Rose Garden
description:
Trump Administration
                The artist behind the piece is also responsible for a MAGA-friendly Trump statue.
body:
Trump Administration
                The artist behind the piece is also responsible for a MAGA-friendly Trump statue. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            The Thomas Jefferson statue from sculptor George Lundeen's home in Loveland, Colorado. (Courtesy George Lundeen).President Donald Trump continues to furnish the White House Rose Garden with statues of his favorite predecessors, most recently adding a bronze of the third US President, Thomas Jefferson. Made by Colorado-based artist George Lundeen, the statue portrays the founding father seated on a bench with a quill in his hand and the Declaration of Independence on his lap. He looks into the distance, as if he's pausing to ponder while authoring the historical document. The Jefferson piece marks the fifth addition to Trump's Rose Garden, which already contains sculptures of George Washington, Alexander Hamilton, Benjamin Franklin, and "Freedom's Charge" — a statue depicting two Revolutionary War soldiers.In a statement to Hyperallergic, Lundeen said that he had completed the statue 25 years ago. "Without Thomas Jefferson, you have to wonder whether there would be a United States of America," he said.The artist also collaborated on a statue of the president holding a "Make America Great Again" hat and pumping the air with his fist — a posture meant to capture Trump's reaction immediately after the 2024 assassination attempt in Butler, Pennsylvania. That piece now resides in Trump's golf club in West Palm Beach, Florida.  Implementing the Jefferson statue is one of Trump's latest efforts to reshape the White House Grounds and DC at large. Since renovations to the Rose Garden began in 2020, Trump has razed the Kennedy-Era Lawn in favor of a Mar-a-Lago-style patio, and installed a "Presidential Walk of Fame" with portraits of all US presidents except for Joe Biden, who was sarcastically replaced with an autopen device.Trump's aesthetic aims extend to other parts of the capital city. In June, six heritage preservation groups based in Washington, DC, sued the Trump administration over its plans to create a "Garden of American Heroes" in West Potomac Park. The garden is meant to include 250 American heroes, from Muhammad Ali and Frederick Douglass, to divisive figures like Christopher Columbus, whose likeness made an earlier appearance in the White House compound in March.
